newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi mourns murdered Hutu president.
newsitem.headline: Burundi mourns murdered Hutu president.

text.p: Burundi on Monday commemorated the third anniversary of the murder of its first democratically elected president Melchior Ndadaye, a Hutu, whose killing by renegade Tutsi troops sparked a civil war.
The ethnic war has left 150,000 dead and is killing 1,000 monthly, aid workers say.

Under tight security, military strongman Major Pierre Buyoya -- the man who handed over power to Melchior Ndadaye in 1993 after being defeated in pluralist elections -- laid a wreath at Ndadaye's grave watched on by members of his government.

Buyoya returned to power on July 25 this year in a bloodless coup which toppled Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya. Ntibantuganya took over from Ndadaye's successor, Cyprien Ntaryamira who was killed in a plane crash in 1994 together with Rwandan president Juvenal Habyarimana.

Ndadaye was machine-gunned to death on October 21, 1993 by renegade Tutsi soldiers. The tiny tea and coffee-growing nation has remained unstable since then after Hutus took up arms to avenge Ndadaye's death and force the Tutsis to share power.
His death marked the end of Burundi's brief experiment with western-style democracy in a country where Tutsis control political and military power despite only being 15 percent of the population.

Ndadaye's death also ignited ethnic violence between the Tutsi-dominated army and the majority Hutus, especially members of his Frodebu party, which has left more than 150,000 dead in the past three years.

Most members of his Frodebu party quit Burundi into exile where they formed a rebel group -- the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) -- which has stepped a war aid workers say is killing 1,000 people monthly.

The speaker of the National Assembly Leonce Ngendakumana, dismissed by Buyoya after the July coup but reinstated recently after pressure from regional leaders who imposed sanctions against Burundi, also laid a wreath on Ndadaye's grave.

The wreath-laying ceremony and a two-hour mass at the Catholic cathedral attended by Buyoya, Ngendakumana, Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira, diplomats and around 1,000 people passed off without a security incident.
"Frodebu will continue to condemn the 25 July 1996 coup with all its strength," the party said in a statement.
Privately Frodebu leaders, who opted to work in legal opposition to Buyoya rather than join Hutu rebels, concede it could take 20 years of transition to resolve Burundi's ethnic divisions.
Buyoya has set himself a minimum three year transitional period, though his army junta has said it would not start negotiations with Hutu rebels until sanctions were lifted.
A committee from regional states who imposed sanctions on Burundi on July 31 opened a meeting in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha on Monday to review the sanctions.

Regional heads of state refused to lift or ease the sanctions at a meeting in Arusha early this month, saying Buyoya had not done enough to resolve the political impasse in ethnically-divided Burundi.
The heads of state want Buyoya to open unconditional talks Leonard Nyangoma's CNDD and other smaller Hutu rebel groups in Burundi.
Ndadaye's anniversary is a source of tension for Buyoya's unrecognised government, which wants to present itself as an administration for all Burundians irrespective of the ethnic divide.
But the capital Bujumbura has been virtually cleansed of Hutus who have fled into exile or the Hutu-controlled countryside -- a no-go area for the Tutsi army and its ethnic supporters.
Regional analysts fear Burundi could go down the same path as neighbouring Rwanda, where a million Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were slaughtered in 1994.
